title: How to find scene cuts with ffmpeg and split the video exactly on them
summary:
ffmpeg can find the cuts in an edited video with one filter, and most guides stop there: select='gt(scene,0.4)',showinfo, read the timestamps, done. On a real edit two things are still open afterwards. Which threshold separates cuts from camera shake, and how do you turn the timestamps into files that actually start on the cut? The video editor in the osFoundry desktop app does the first half in Rust (canvas_scene_split in canvas_operations.rs) and avoids the second half entirely. Below, both halves are rebuilt in Python and measured on one video, with the numbers that decide each choice.

The test file is NASA's public-domain launch highlights from the Artemis II test flight: 92 seconds of H.264 at 640×360, 30 fps, 2,760 frames, cut from 19 shots. All timings are from an Apple M1 with ffmpeg 7.1 and Python 3.9.

Detecting the cuts

The command is the one every guide shows. The detail that costs people an afternoon is where the output goes: showinfo writes to ffmpeg's log, which is stderr. Read stdout and you get an empty list from a run that worked.

import re, subprocess

def detect(video, threshold):
    vf = f"select='gt(scene,{threshold})',showinfo"
    p = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-i", video, "-an",
                        "-filter_complex", vf, "-f", "null", "-"],
                       capture_output=True, text=True)
    return [round(float(t) * 1000)
            for t in re.findall(r"pts_time:([0-9.]+)", p.stderr)]

At 0.27, the app's default, this returns 18 cut times in milliseconds, from 3,133 to 73,033. The pass took 0.80 s (median of 5 runs), so detection is cheap enough to rerun with a different threshold whenever you like.

What the scene score measures

The threshold is easier to pick once you know what the number is. In libavfilter/f_select.c, get_scene_score computes the mean absolute difference between this frame and the previous one (mafd), then subtracts the previous frame's mafd:

score = min(mafd, |mafd - prev_mafd|) / 100

For YUV input only the luma plane is compared. That makes the score easy to rebuild in a few lines of Python, which is the quickest way to understand a surprising value:

def luma(video, n):
    p = subprocess.run(["ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-i", video,
                        "-vf", f"select='eq(n,{n})'", "-frames:v", "1",
                        "-f", "rawvideo", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-"],
                       capture_output=True)
    return p.stdout[:640 * 360]   # Y plane only

def mafd(a, b):
    return sum(abs(x - y) for x, y in zip(a, b)) / len(a)

f0, f1, f2 = (luma(VIDEO, k) for k in (n - 2, n - 1, n))
prev, cur = mafd(f0, f1), mafd(f1, f2)
score = min(cur, abs(cur - prev)) / 100

Taking the Y plane from yuv420p rather than asking for -pix_fmt gray matters: the gray conversion stretches the value range and the rebuilt scores came out about 16 % too high. With the raw Y plane, four frames from this video match ffmpeg's own scores:

frame what happens mafd previous mafd score
33.300 s hard cut to the crowd 57.12 1.31 0.558
33.333 s the frame after that cut 13.75 57.12 0.138
58.567 s camera shake at engine ignition 27.03 10.88 0.161
63.667 s cut from the pad to a wide sky shot 34.64 0.90 0.337

The subtraction is what keeps moving shots from firing. The ignition frame differs from the one before it by 27 brightness levels on average, twice as much as the frame after the crowd cut. But the frame before it had already changed by 10.9, so only the increase counts, and it scores 0.16. The cut from the pad to the sky changes less than many cuts do, but it follows a nearly still frame, so it scores 0.34. A cut is a jump in change, not just a lot of change.

Picking the threshold from the data

Instead of guessing, dump the score of every frame once and look at where the gap is:

ffmpeg -i launch.mp4 -an -vf "select='gte(scene,0)',metadata=print:file=-" -f null - \
  | grep -o 'scene_score=[0-9.]*'

The median frame of this video scores 0.0015. Seventeen frames score above 0.5, one scores 0.337, and the next highest is the ignition frame at 0.161. Any threshold between 0.162 and 0.337 returns the same 18 cuts. The sweep, with and without a 500 ms minimum gap between cuts:

threshold frames over it cuts after 500 ms gap
0.08 27 20
0.10 24 20
0.12 20 19
0.15 19 19
0.20 18 18
0.27 18 18
0.35 17 17
0.40 17 17
0.50 17 17

Most of the 0.3–0.5 range that the ffmpeg mailing list and many tutorials suggest is too high for this video: at 0.35 and above, the pad-to-sky cut is gone. At 0.15 and below, the ignition starts producing cuts. On footage with a lot of fast motion the safe band can be narrow, so it's worth one look at the distribution before trusting a number from someone else's video.

The minimum gap

The rows at 0.08 to 0.12 show why the app drops hits that come too soon after the previous one (parse_scene_times, 500 ms by default). At 0.12, the cut at 33.300 s fires again on the next frame at 33.333 s, because that frame still differs from its neighbour by 13.75 while the jump before it was huge. At 0.08, the ignition produces eight hits between 57.7 s and 59.0 s. A gap of half a second collapses each burst into one marker:

def min_gap(hits, gap_ms=500):
    out = []
    for ms in hits:
        if not out or ms - out[-1] >= gap_ms:
            out.append(ms)
    return out

It doesn't fix a low threshold, only the duplicates. At 0.08 the gap still leaves two false cuts in the ignition.

Splitting with -c copy doesn't land on the cuts

The obvious next step is ffmpeg's segment muxer with stream copy:

ffmpeg -i launch.mp4 -c copy -f segment -segment_times 3.133,6.333,... \
  -reset_timestamps 1 scene%02d.mp4

It took 0.05 s and produced 18 files, not 19, all between 3.3 and 6.0 seconds long. The scenes themselves run from 1.5 to 19.0 seconds. A stream copy can only start a file on a keyframe, and this encode has 18 of them, at most 6 seconds apart. ffprobe -skip_frame nokey lists them:

ffprobe -v error -select_streams v -skip_frame nokey \
  -show_entries frame=pts_time -of csv=p=0 launch.mp4

Only 5 of the 18 cuts fall on a keyframe, the ones where the original encoder happened to place one. Every other file boundary comes late, the worst by about 4 seconds, and where two cuts share the same next keyframe they collapse into one boundary.

Re-encoding, and the half-frame trap

Re-encoding with a keyframe forced at each cut makes the boundaries free to land anywhere:

ffmpeg -i launch.mp4 -c:v libx264 -crf 18 -preset fast -c:a aac \
  -force_key_frames "$T" -f segment -segment_times "$T" \
  -reset_timestamps 1 scene%02d.mp4

With $T set to the detected times rounded to milliseconds, this produced 19 files, and 4 of the 18 cuts were still one frame late. One cut was missed entirely, merging two scenes into a 12.3-second file, and a stray file held a single frame. The cause is rounding. A cut at frame 269 is at 8.9666… s, and "8.967" lies just after it, so the comparison picks the next frame. All four late cuts sit at times ending in a repeating 6, and so does the stray frame at 44.067 s.

Moving every time half a frame earlier (1/60 s at 30 fps) puts it unambiguously before the cut frame:

T = ",".join(f"{ms / 1000 - 0.5 / 30:.4f}" for ms in cuts)

With that change, all 18 boundaries landed on the cut frame and the 19 file lengths matched the scene lengths to the frame. The re-encode took 6.9 s for the 92-second clip and wrote 15.2 MB, against 18.2 MB for the source at CRF 18.

Or don't write files at all

The app takes the third route. Its Split at buttons call canvas_split_clip in canvas_layers.rs, which shortens the selected clip and inserts a new clip on the same asset with a later in-point. Nothing is decoded or written, so there is no keyframe problem and no generation loss, and the encode happens once, when the finished edit is exported. If the goal is to recut the video rather than to hand someone 19 files, that's the version to copy: keep the cut list as in/out points and let the final render do the frame-accurate work.

The full script, with every measurement above, is about 120 lines of standard-library Python around ffmpeg and ffprobe. In the osFoundry desktop app the same detection is the Find the cuts preset in the video editor, and it runs on your own machine as described on the local-first page. The app is free from the osFoundry download page.

title: How to remove silence from a recording in Python without clipping words
summary:
Removing the pauses from a voice recording comes down to four numbers: a level below which audio counts as silent, how long a quiet stretch must last before it is removed, and how much to keep on either side of each piece that survives. The Sound Editor in the osFoundry desktop app exposes exactly these four in its Strip Silence dialog, with defaults of −48 dB, 50 ms, 5 ms and 20 ms. Below, the same operation is rebuilt in about 40 lines of numpy, checked sample for sample against a file the app exported, and then used to measure what each number actually does. At the end, the same job with ffmpeg's silenceremove, which behaves differently in a way that is easy to miss.

The test recordings

Two test takes, built for this: five short text-to-speech sentences each (English and Japanese), separated by 2.4 to 3.4 seconds of quiet, with generated room hiss underneath. 48 kHz, mono, 16-bit.

take length hiss RMS hiss peak
English 27.57 s −64.6 dBFS −52.4 dBFS
Japanese 33.55 s −64.6 dBFS −52.4 dBFS

The gap between those last two columns matters later. Hiss that averages −64.6 dBFS still has individual samples reaching −52.4.

The rule

A sample is quiet if its absolute value is at or below the threshold. A run of quiet samples is strippable if it lasts at least the minimum length. Everything between strippable runs becomes a clip, widened by the start and end pads:

import numpy as np

def silent_runs(x, sr, threshold_db, min_ms):
    quiet = np.abs(x) <= 10 ** (threshold_db / 20)
    edges = np.flatnonzero(np.diff(np.concatenate(([0], quiet.view(np.int8), [0]))))
    runs = edges.reshape(-1, 2)  # [start, end) of every quiet run
    keep = (runs[:, 1] - runs[:, 0]) >= min_ms * sr / 1000
    keep |= (runs[:, 0] == 0) | (runs[:, 1] == len(x))  # file edges: always strippable
    return runs[keep]

def strip_silence(x, sr, threshold_db=-48, min_ms=50, pad_start_ms=5, pad_end_ms=20):
    runs = silent_runs(x, sr, threshold_db, min_ms)
    bounds = np.concatenate(([0], runs.ravel(), [len(x)])).reshape(-1, 2)
    ps, pe = int(pad_start_ms * sr / 1000), int(pad_end_ms * sr / 1000)
    clips = []
    for s, e in bounds:
        if e <= s:
            continue
        s, e = max(0, s - ps), min(len(x), e + pe)
        if clips and s <= clips[-1][1]:  # pads made two clips touch: merge
            clips[-1][1] = e
        else:
            clips.append([s, e])
    return clips

Stripping only removes. Closing the gaps is a separate step, the one the Sound Editor calls Space Clips: put the clips end to start, leaving the first one where it was.

def space_clips(x, clips):
    return np.concatenate([np.zeros(clips[0][0], x.dtype)] + [x[s:e] for s, e in clips])

Checking it against the app

Both takes went through the Sound Editor with −48 dB, 500 ms, 100 ms and 300 ms, then Space Clips, then Bounce Mix normalized to −0.1 dBFS. The app's file is 24-bit stereo with identical channels. Comparing it with the numpy result, normalized the same way:

take app bounce numpy largest difference
English 660,500 samples (13.76 s) 660,500 samples −135.0 dB
Japanese 815,030 samples (16.98 s) 815,030 samples −132.5 dB

Same length to the sample, and differences at the level of 24-bit rounding. A plain per-sample comparison, no RMS window and no smoothing, is enough to reproduce what the app exports.

The first version of the rebuild was off by exactly one region, and it is the one place where a naive implementation goes wrong. Each take starts with 0.47 seconds of quiet before the first word, shorter than the 500 ms minimum. Applied literally, the rule keeps it, and the output starts with 0.47 s of hiss. The app's file instead starts with 0.376 s of digital zero, then the first word: quiet touching the start or end of the file is stripped whatever its length, and the first clip keeps its position (0.47 s minus the 100 ms start pad). That is the keep |= line above.

Minimum length decides the shape

With the default pads (5 ms and 20 ms), only the minimum length changes:

min strip duration English clips English output Japanese clips Japanese output
20 ms 18 11.40 s 19 14.08 s
50 ms (default) 11 11.46 s 14 14.15 s
100 ms 7 11.63 s 11 14.30 s
200 ms 6 11.73 s 6 15.00 s
300 ms 5 11.98 s 5 15.20 s
500 ms 5 11.98 s 5 15.20 s

Both takes have five sentences. At the default 50 ms the English take comes back as 11 clips and the Japanese as 14: the short gaps inside sentences (6 of them between 50 and 500 ms in the English take, 9 in the Japanese) count as silence and are cut out. The output is only half a second shorter than at 500 ms, but every one of those cuts removes a breath or the space between two words, and the result sounds clipped. From 300 ms up, each take is exactly five clips, one per sentence. The total length barely moves; what changes is where the cuts are.

Pads decide the rhythm

With the minimum at 500 ms, the pads:

start / end pad English output Japanese output
0 / 0 ms 11.86 s 15.08 s
5 / 20 ms 11.98 s 15.20 s
50 / 100 ms 12.56 s 15.78 s
100 / 300 ms 13.76 s 16.98 s
200 / 500 ms 15.16 s 18.38 s

After the gaps are closed, the pause between two sentences is the end pad of one plus the start pad of the next. At 0/0 the sentences butt against each other; at 100/300 every join is a 0.4-second breath, which is roughly what a speaker leaves when reading at a steady pace. The start pad does a second job: soft word onsets are often below the threshold, and without it the first consonant of a sentence is gone. The end pad is the one to tune by ear.

The threshold has to clear the noise peaks, not its average

With 500 ms and 100/300 pads, sweeping the threshold:

threshold English clips English output Japanese clips Japanese output
−36 dB 5 13.29 s 5 16.79 s
−40 dB 5 13.34 s 5 16.87 s
−44 dB 5 13.40 s 5 16.94 s
−48 dB 5 13.76 s 5 16.98 s
−52 dB 10 17.48 s 13 22.78 s
−56 dB 1 27.57 s 1 33.55 s

From −36 to −48 dB the result is stable; a higher threshold only trims a little more of each word's quiet tail. At −52 dB, just above the hiss peaks, occasional hiss samples cross the line and break the long pauses into pieces shorter than 500 ms, so several of them survive. At −56 dB the hiss counts as sound everywhere and nothing is stripped at all. −56 looks like a safe choice if you only know the noise floor is around −64 dB RMS. Because the rule compares single samples, what matters is the hiss's peak, and the threshold needs a few dB of room above it.

The same job with ffmpeg

ffmpeg has two relevant filters. silencedetect only reports, and with the same threshold and minimum it finds the same pauses as the rebuild:

ffmpeg -i en-take.wav -af silencedetect=noise=-48dB:d=0.5 -f null - 2>&1 | grep silence_
# silence_start: 2.411833
# silence_end: 6.070167 | silence_duration: 3.658333
# ...

The first sentence ends at 2.4118 s, and the rebuild's first clip ends at 2.712 s, the same point plus the 300 ms end pad. Note what is missing from that output: the 0.47 s of quiet at the start of the file, shorter than d, is not reported.

silenceremove cuts directly, and this is where expectations go wrong. With ffmpeg 7.1:

ffmpeg -i en-take.wav -af "silenceremove=start_periods=1:start_threshold=-48dB:\
stop_periods=-1:stop_threshold=-48dB:stop_duration=0.5:stop_silence=0:detection=peak" out.wav
filter settings English output Japanese output
detection=peak, stop_silence=0 13.98 s 17.20 s
detection=peak, stop_silence=0.3 15.48 s 18.70 s
detection=rms, stop_silence=0 13.50 s 17.03 s
numpy, 500 ms, pads 0/0 11.86 s 15.08 s

With stop_silence=0 the output is still about 2 seconds longer than a zero-pad strip. Running silencedetect on it shows why: each removed pause has left about 0.52 s behind. stop_duration is both the minimum length and the amount of silence the filter lets through before it starts cutting, so asking for "only remove pauses over 500 ms" also means "leave 500 ms of each one". stop_silence then adds to that rather than replacing it, and there is no option for padding before speech. If the pauses should come out at a chosen length, silencedetect plus your own cut list (or the numpy version above) gives that control; silenceremove is fine when a half-second pause is what you wanted anyway.

The full script with every sweep above is about 90 lines of Python with numpy and soundfile. In the osFoundry desktop app, the same steps are Edit → Strip Silence and Edit → Space Clips… in the Sound Editor, running on your own machine in line with the app's local-first design. The app is free from the osFoundry download page.

    bounds = np.concatenate(([0], runs.ravel(), [len(x)])).reshape(-1, 2)
    ps, pe = int(pad_start_ms * sr / 1000), int(pad_end_ms * sr / 1000)
    clips = []
    for s, e in bounds:
        if e <= s:
            continue
        s, e = max(0, s - ps), min(len(x), e + pe)
        if clips and s <= clips[-1][1]:  # pads made two clips touch: merge
            clips[-1][1] = e
        else:
            clips.append([s, e])
    return clips

Stripping only removes. Closing the gaps is a separate step, the one the Sound Editor calls Space Clips: put the clips end to start, leaving the first one where it was.

def space_clips(x, clips):
    return np.concatenate([np.zeros(clips[0][0], x.dtype)] + [x[s:e] for s, e in clips])

Checking it against the app

Both takes went through the Sound Editor with −48 dB, 500 ms, 100 ms and 300 ms, then Space Clips, then Bounce Mix normalized to −0.1 dBFS. The app's file is 24-bit stereo with identical channels. Comparing it with the numpy result, normalized the same way:

take app bounce numpy largest difference
English 660,500 samples (13.76 s) 660,500 samples −135.0 dB
Japanese 815,030 samples (16.98 s) 815,030 samples −132.5 dB

Same length to the sample, and differences at the level of 24-bit rounding. A plain per-sample comparison, no RMS window and no smoothing, is enough to reproduce what the app exports.

The first version of the rebuild was off by exactly one region, and it is the one place where a naive implementation goes wrong. Each take starts with 0.47 seconds of quiet before the first word, shorter than the 500 ms minimum. Applied literally, the rule keeps it, and the output starts with 0.47 s of hiss. The app's file instead starts with 0.376 s of digital zero, then the first word: quiet touching the start or end of the file is stripped whatever its length, and the first clip keeps its position (0.47 s minus the 100 ms start pad). That is the keep |= line above.

Minimum length decides the shape

With the default pads (5 ms and 20 ms), only the minimum length changes:

min strip duration English clips English output Japanese clips Japanese output
20 ms 18 11.40 s 19 14.08 s
50 ms (default) 11 11.46 s 14 14.15 s
100 ms 7 11.63 s 11 14.30 s
200 ms 6 11.73 s 6 15.00 s
300 ms 5 11.98 s 5 15.20 s
500 ms 5 11.98 s 5 15.20 s

Both takes have five sentences. At the default 50 ms the English take comes back as 11 clips and the Japanese as 14: the short gaps inside sentences (6 of them between 50 and 500 ms in the English take, 9 in the Japanese) count as silence and are cut out. The output is only half a second shorter than at 500 ms, but every one of those cuts removes a breath or the space between two words, and the result sounds clipped. From 300 ms up, each take is exactly five clips, one per sentence. The total length barely moves; what changes is where the cuts are.

Pads decide the rhythm

With the minimum at 500 ms, the pads:

start / end pad English output Japanese output
0 / 0 ms 11.86 s 15.08 s
5 / 20 ms 11.98 s 15.20 s
50 / 100 ms 12.56 s 15.78 s
100 / 300 ms 13.76 s 16.98 s
200 / 500 ms 15.16 s 18.38 s

After the gaps are closed, the pause between two sentences is the end pad of one plus the start pad of the next. At 0/0 the sentences butt against each other; at 100/300 every join is a 0.4-second breath, which is roughly what a speaker leaves when reading at a steady pace. The start pad does a second job: soft word onsets are often below the threshold, and without it the first consonant of a sentence is gone. The end pad is the one to tune by ear.

The threshold has to clear the noise peaks, not its average

With 500 ms and 100/300 pads, sweeping the threshold:

threshold English clips English output Japanese clips Japanese output
−36 dB 5 13.29 s 5 16.79 s
−40 dB 5 13.34 s 5 16.87 s
−44 dB 5 13.40 s 5 16.94 s
−48 dB 5 13.76 s 5 16.98 s
−52 dB 10 17.48 s 13 22.78 s
−56 dB 1 27.57 s 1 33.55 s

From −36 to −48 dB the result is stable; a higher threshold only trims a little more of each word's quiet tail. At −52 dB, just above the hiss peaks, occasional hiss samples cross the line and break the long pauses into pieces shorter than 500 ms, so several of them survive. At −56 dB the hiss counts as sound everywhere and nothing is stripped at all. −56 looks like a safe choice if you only know the noise floor is around −64 dB RMS. Because the rule compares single samples, what matters is the hiss's peak, and the threshold needs a few dB of room above it.

The same job with ffmpeg

ffmpeg has two relevant filters. silencedetect only reports, and with the same threshold and minimum it finds the same pauses as the rebuild:

ffmpeg -i en-take.wav -af silencedetect=noise=-48dB:d=0.5 -f null - 2>&1 | grep silence_
# silence_start: 2.411833
# silence_end: 6.070167 | silence_duration: 3.658333
# ...

The first sentence ends at 2.4118 s, and the rebuild's first clip ends at 2.712 s, the same point plus the 300 ms end pad. Note what is missing from that output: the 0.47 s of quiet at the start of the file, shorter than d, is not reported.

silenceremove cuts directly, and this is where expectations go wrong. With ffmpeg 7.1:

ffmpeg -i en-take.wav -af "silenceremove=start_periods=1:start_threshold=-48dB:\
stop_periods=-1:stop_threshold=-48dB:stop_duration=0.5:stop_silence=0:detection=peak" out.wav
filter settings English output Japanese output
detection=peak, stop_silence=0 13.98 s 17.20 s
detection=peak, stop_silence=0.3 15.48 s 18.70 s
detection=rms, stop_silence=0 13.50 s 17.03 s
numpy, 500 ms, pads 0/0 11.86 s 15.08 s

With stop_silence=0 the output is still about 2 seconds longer than a zero-pad strip. Running silencedetect on it shows why: each removed pause has left about 0.52 s behind. stop_duration is both the minimum length and the amount of silence the filter lets through before it starts cutting, so asking for "only remove pauses over 500 ms" also means "leave 500 ms of each one". stop_silence then adds to that rather than replacing it, and there is no option for padding before speech. If the pauses should come out at a chosen length, silencedetect plus your own cut list (or the numpy version above) gives that control; silenceremove is fine when a half-second pause is what you wanted anyway.

The full script with every sweep above is about 90 lines of Python with numpy and soundfile. In the osFoundry desktop app, the same steps are Edit → Strip Silence and Edit → Space Clips… in the Sound Editor, running on your own machine in line with the app's local-first design. The app is free from the osFoundry download page.

title: Cara menemukan feed atau halaman rubrik situs berita dari robots.txt dan sitemap dengan Python
summary:
Tugas pertama sebuah feed reader adalah menemukan feed-nya, dan di banyak situs berita besar feed itu memang tidak ada. Jalan pintas yang biasa dipakai orang adalah scraping halaman depan, yang rapuh dan tidak sopan. Ada urutan langkah yang lebih baik, dan sebagian besar sudah diumumkan oleh situs itu sendiri: di tag , di robots.txt, dan di sitemap. Aplikasi desktop osFoundry melakukan ini dengan Rust (news_feed.rs, fungsi news_discover_feeds, news_discover_sections dan news_fetch_section). Di bawah ini prosedur yang sama dalam Python dengan standard library saja, dijalankan terhadap delapan situs berita sungguhan, lengkap dengan jumlah request yang dihabiskan tiap situs dan di mana hasil akhirnya.

Aturan dasar sebelum request pertama

Skrip discovery mengakses situs yang belum pernah ia lihat, jadi sopan santunnya harus tertanam di satu fungsi yang membuat request, bukan diserahkan ke pemanggil.

UA = "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; osFoundryNews/1.0; +https://osfoundry.io)"
PAUSE = 1.0          # seconds between requests to the same site
MAX_REQUESTS = 25    # per site, everything included

class Site:
    def __init__(self, host):
        self.root = f"https://{host}/"
        self.log, self.robots, self._last = [], None, 0.0

    def get(self, url, step):
        if len(self.log) >= MAX_REQUESTS:
            raise Budget(url)
        if self.robots and not url.endswith("/robots.txt") and not self.robots.can_fetch(UA, url):
            self.log.append((step, url, "robots-disallow", 0, 0))
            return None, None
        wait = self._last + PAUSE - time.monotonic()
        if wait > 0:
            time.sleep(wait)
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA, "Accept-Encoding": "gzip"})
        status, body = None, None
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=15) as r:
                raw = r.read(8 * 1024 * 1024)
                if r.headers.get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip" or url.endswith(".gz"):
                    raw = gzip.decompress(raw)
                status, body = r.status, raw.decode("utf-8", "replace")
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
            status = e.code
        except Exception as e:
            status = type(e).__name__
        self._last = time.monotonic()
        self.log.append((step, url, status, len(body or ""), round((self._last - t0) * 1000)))
        return status, body

Satu request dalam satu waktu, jaraknya minimal satu detik, batas keras per situs, User-Agent yang menyebutkan siapa yang bertanya (sama dengan yang dikirim aplikasi), dan robots.txt dicek lewat urllib.robotparser sebelum setiap URL lain. Log inilah sumber semua angka di bawah.

robots.txt diambil paling awal, sebelum halaman depan. Di situs yang ternyata punya feed, ini memakan satu request tambahan, tapi dengan begitu aturannya berlaku untuk semua request sesudahnya, dan file itu juga memuat daftar sitemap yang memang dibutuhkan di langkah berikutnya. Ada dua kondisi berhenti lagi di atasnya: kalau robots.txt melarang root situs untuk User-Agent ini, atau halaman depan menjawab 401, 403 atau 429, skrip berhenti untuk situs itu.

Langkah 1: feed yang diumumkan situs

Situs yang punya RSS hampir selalu menyebutkannya di head halaman. Satu request untuk halaman depan, satu kali parsing HTML:

class Links(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.alternates, self.anchors = [], []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        a = dict(attrs)
        if tag == "link" and "alternate" in (a.get("rel") or "").lower().split():
            t = (a.get("type") or "").lower()
            if ("rss" in t or "atom" in t) and a.get("href"):
                self.alternates.append(a["href"])
        elif tag == "a" and a.get("href"):
            self.anchors.append(a["href"])

Di The Verge, TechCrunch dan ITmedia, urusannya selesai di sini: masing-masing dua request (robots.txt dan halaman depan), beres dalam kurang dari 4 detik termasuk jeda. Feed ITmedia ada di host lain (rss.itmedia.co.jp), dan itu salah satu alasan untuk lebih percaya pada link yang diumumkan daripada menebak path.

Langkah 2: sembilan alamat yang umum

Kalau tidak ada yang diumumkan, aplikasi mencoba sembilan path feed yang umum dan berhenti di path pertama yang bisa di-parse sebagai RSS atau Atom: /feed, /feed/, /rss, /rss.xml, /feed.xml, /atom.xml, /index.xml, /feeds/posts/default, /rss/index.xml. Path ini menangkap default CMS (WordPress, Blogger, Hugo, Ghost) di situs yang tema-nya lupa memasang tag .

Di tiga koran nasional Jepang dalam pengujian ini, Nikkei, Asahi dan Yomiuri, ke-27 percobaan gagal: 26 menjawab 404 dan satu (asahi.com/rss) menjawab 403. Itu 9 dari 13 atau 14 request yang dihabiskan tiap situs. Kalau Anda hanya peduli pada penerbit besar, membaca sitemap sebelum percobaan ini akan memangkas tiap run menjadi 4 atau 5 request. Untuk tool umum yang juga harus menangani blog kecil, percobaan ini tetap layak dipertahankan.

Langkah 3: apa yang ditunjuk robots.txt

robots.txt mencantumkan sitemap lewat baris Sitemap:. Sebuah sitemap bisa berupa yang menunjuk ke sitemap lain, atau berisi halaman. Skrip membaca hingga empat sitemap yang tercantum, masuk satu level ke dalam index (hingga lima anak), dan berhenti di sitemap pertama yang bisa dipakai.

Menentukan sitemap mana yang bisa dipakai adalah bagian yang perlu hati-hati. Tes yang paling jelas adalah namespace Google News, xmlns:news=, yang oleh format ini dikhususkan untuk artikel yang baru terbit. Nikkei menunjukkan kenapa tes itu tidak cukup. sections_sitemap.xml miliknya mendeklarasikan namespace tersebut, padahal 184 dari 187 URL-nya adalah halaman rubrik seperti /business/startups/. Jadi skrip menilai sitemap dari URL di dalamnya:

def usable(info):
    """Judge a sitemap by the URLs in it, not by the namespace it declares."""
    if info.get("section_share", 0) >= 0.7:
        return "sections"
    if info.get("article_share", 0) >= 0.7 and info["kind"] == "news_sitemap":
        return "news sitemap"
    if info.get("article_share", 0) >= 0.7 and info.get("dated"):
        return "article sitemap"
    return None

section_share dan article_share adalah proporsi path yang lolos dua tes bentuk di bawah. Ambang 70 % adalah angka yang dipakai aplikasi untuk sitemap rubrik.

Berikut hasil akhir tiap situs:

Situs Request Detik Hasil akhir
www.theverge.com 2 3.7 RSS dari
techcrunch.com 2 3.4 RSS dari
www.itmedia.co.jp 2 3.6 RSS dari (di rss.itmedia.co.jp)
www.yomiuri.co.jp 13 27.2 News sitemap, 340 artikel, semuanya dari 24 jam terakhir
www.asahi.com 13 47.3 News sitemap (national), 61 artikel, 36 dari 24 jam terakhir
www.nikkei.com 14 30.8 Sitemap rubrik, 184 rubrik; halaman Startups menghasilkan 20 artikel
apnews.com 2 2.9 Berhenti: halaman depan menjawab 403
www.reuters.com 1 1.5 Berhenti: robots.txt melarang User-Agent ini

Diukur dari sebuah Mac pada November 2026, satu situs demi satu situs. Sebagian besar detiknya berasal dari jeda satu detik; respons tunggal paling lambat adalah 6.9 s, yaitu 403 dari asahi.com/rss.

Yomiuri dan Asahi tidak butuh apa-apa lagi: news sitemap pada dasarnya adalah feed tanpa ringkasan, berisi URL, judul dan waktu terbit untuk tiap artikel. Index milik Asahi memecahnya per desk redaksi (sitemap_national.xml, sitemap_business.xml dan seterusnya), jadi mengikutinya berarti memilih desk, mirip dengan memilih rubrik.

Langkah 4: halaman rubrik, kalau hanya itu yang ada

Sitemap Nikkei lebih mirip direktori situs daripada daftar artikel. Tes bentuk untuk rubrik adalah kebalikan dari tes artikel, ditambah batas kedalaman dan blocklist pendek:

def looks_like_article(path):
    segs = [s for s in path.split("/") if s]
    if not segs:
        return False
    last = re.sub(r"(\.html?)+$", "", segs[-1])
    if len(last) < 6:
        return False
    if len(segs) < 2:
        return last.count("-") >= 3
    if any(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", a) and re.fullmatch(r"\d{2}", b) for a, b in zip(segs, segs[1:])):
        return True
    if len(last) >= 8 and re.search(r"\d", last):
        return True
    return last.count("-") >= 3

def looks_like_section(path):
    if looks_like_article(path):
        return False
    segs = [s for s in path.split("/") if s]
    if not segs or len(segs) > 3:
        return False
    if "." in segs[-1] and not segs[-1].endswith(".html"):
        return False
    return not any(s.lower() in BLOCKED for s in segs)   # search, login, about, privacy, ...

Sebuah artikel adalah path yang mengandung pasangan tanggal (/2026/11/06/), segmen terakhir mirip ID sepanjang 8 karakter atau lebih yang mengandung angka, atau slug dengan minimal tiga tanda hubung. Aturan ID tidak diterapkan di kedalaman 1, karena di sana aturan itu akan ikut menelan halaman tag seperti /coronavirus-2026. Tiga tanda hubung, bukan dua, karena /news/tech-and-science/ adalah rubrik di banyak situs.

Mengikuti sebuah rubrik lalu cukup satu request per pengecekan: ambil halaman rubrik, simpan link ke host yang sama yang berbentuk artikel, dan buang yang nyasar.

shaped = [u for u in unique if looks_like_article(urlparse(u).path)]
first = lambda u: next((s for s in urlparse(u).path.split("/") if s), None)
counts = {}
for u in shaped:
    counts[first(u)] = counts.get(first(u), 0) + 1
if counts:
    seg, n = max(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1])
    if n * 10 >= len(shaped) * 6:
        shaped = [u for u in shaped if first(u) == seg]

Halaman Startups Nikkei punya 271 link berbeda ke host yang sama. Tes bentuk dan aturan segmen dominan (kalau 60 % hasil yang cocok diawali segmen pertama yang sama, di sini /article/, sisanya dibuang) menyisakan 20, semuanya berbentuk /article/DGXZQOUC026TI0S6A101C2000000/. 251 yang dibuang adalah menu, halaman tag dan tema, /login, /search, halaman data pasar dan sejenisnya.

Aplikasi sampai di titik yang sama. Pemilih rubriknya untuk www.nikkei.com menampilkan "Showing 60 of 185 sections": 184 dari sitemap ditambah halaman depan, yang baru ditambahkan setelah dicek bahwa halaman depan itu sendiri memuat link artikel.

Satu hal lagi yang dibocorkan sitemap rubrik Nikkei: setiap rubrik punya , dan 157 dari 187 berubah dalam 24 jam sebelumnya. Follower yang memantau banyak rubrik bisa membaca satu file itu dulu dan melewati halaman rubrik yang tidak berubah.

Kalau jawabannya tidak

AP menjawab 403 untuk halaman depan, jadi skrip berhenti setelah dua request. Tanpa aturan itu, skrip akan lanjut membuat 13 request lagi yang juga mengembalikan 403, seperti yang terjadi pada versi skrip ini sebelumnya. robots.txt milik Reuters mencantumkan crawler tertentu yang diizinkan dan melarang semua yang lain, jadi skrip berhenti setelah satu request dan tidak pernah mengambil halaman depan.

Keduanya bukan teka-teki yang perlu diakali. Situs yang menjawab 403 ke klien yang sudah mengidentifikasi diri, atau berkata tidak di robots.txt, sudah menjawab pertanyaannya. Perilaku yang berguna bagi tool feed adalah menyampaikannya dengan jelas lalu berhenti, sehingga situs hanya menanggung satu atau dua request, bukan crawl penuh.

Aplikasi desktop osFoundry menjalankan discovery ini secara lokal saat Anda menambahkan sumber di layar News; halaman news firehose menjelaskan apa lagi yang bisa dilakukan layar tersebut.

www.itmedia.co.jp 2 3.6 RSS dari (di rss.itmedia.co.jp)
www.yomiuri.co.jp 13 27.2 News sitemap, 340 artikel, semuanya dari 24 jam terakhir
www.asahi.com 13 47.3 News sitemap (national), 61 artikel, 36 dari 24 jam terakhir
www.nikkei.com 14 30.8 Sitemap rubrik, 184 rubrik; halaman Startups menghasilkan 20 artikel

Diukur dari sebuah Mac pada November 2026, satu situs demi satu situs. Sebagian besar detiknya berasal dari jeda satu detik; respons tunggal paling lambat adalah 6.9 s, yaitu 403 dari asahi.com/rss.

Langkah 4: halaman rubrik, kalau hanya itu yang ada

Sitemap Nikkei lebih mirip direktori situs daripada daftar artikel. Tes bentuk untuk rubrik adalah kebalikan dari tes artikel, ditambah batas kedalaman dan blocklist pendek:

def looks_like_article(path):
    segs = [s for s in path.split("/") if s]
    if not segs:
        return False
    last = re.sub(r"(\.html?)+$", "", segs[-1])
    if len(last) < 6:
        return False
    if len(segs) < 2:
        return last.count("-") >= 3
    if any(re.fullmatch(r"\d{4}", a) and re.fullmatch(r"\d{2}", b) for a, b in zip(segs, segs[1:])):
        return True
    if len(last) >= 8 and re.search(r"\d", last):
        return True
    return last.count("-") >= 3

    if looks_like_article(path):
        return False
    segs = [s for s in path.split("/") if s]
    if not segs or len(segs) > 3:
        return False
    if "." in segs[-1] and not segs[-1].endswith(".html"):

shaped = [u for u in unique if looks_like_article(urlparse(u).path)]

    counts[first(u)] = counts.get(first(u), 0) + 1
if counts:

Aplikasi sampai di titik yang sama. Pemilih rubriknya untuk www.nikkei.com menampilkan "Showing 60 of 185 sections": 184 dari sitemap ditambah halaman depan, yang baru ditambahkan setelah dicek bahwa halaman depan itu sendiri memuat link artikel.

AP menjawab 403 untuk halaman depan, jadi skrip berhenti setelah dua request. Perilaku yang berguna bagi tool feed adalah menyampaikannya dengan jelas lalu berhenti, sehingga situs hanya menanggung satu atau dua request, bukan crawl penuh.

Aplikasi desktop osFoundry menjalankan discovery ini secara lokal saat Anda menambahkan sumber di layar News; halaman news firehose menjelaskan apa lagi yang bisa dilakukan layar tersebut.

title: Why Converted PDF Tables Break in Excel and Word (And How to Fix '=SUM() = 0')
summary:
Every developer, financial analyst, or accountant who has ever tried to extract data from a PDF invoice or bank statement has run into this infuriating scenario:

You convert the PDF table into an Excel spreadsheet or Word document. The grid looks visually acceptable. You highlight the total column, type =SUM(E2:E50), press Enter... and Excel returns 0.

Or worse: numbers with commas turn into dates, negative numbers in accounting parentheses like (1,250.00) get treated as plain text, and multi-line descriptions spill across three independent rows, throwing every debit and credit out of alignment.

Why does converting PDF tables into editable documents fail so consistently, and what is the underlying engineering fix?

1. The Architectural Illusion: PDFs Have No Concept of "Tables"

In HTML, a table is a rigid semantic hierarchy: contains , which contains
.

In the Adobe PDF specification (ISO 32000), tables do not exist.

A PDF is essentially a visual canvas program written in PostScript-derived display commands. When you see a financial table in a PDF, the file actually contains:

  1. Isolated vector stroke instructions (m for move-to, l for line-to, s for stroke) that draw black lines on the page.
  2. Floating text operators (BT, Tf, Td, Tj, ET) that place character glyphs at absolute two-dimensional coordinate positions $(x, y)$. 
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| VISUAL PERCEPTION (A Clean 3-Column Table)                  |
| Date        | Description            | Amount               |
| 2026-11-01  | Cloud Hosting Server   | $1,450.00            |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
                              vs
+-------------------------------------------------------------+
| PDF INTERNAL DATA STREAM (Raw Coordinate Paints)            |
| 0.5 w  72.0 450.0 m  520.0 450.0 l S  (Draws top horizontal)|
| 72.0 440.0 Td (2026-11-01) Tj          (Paints string at x,y) |
| 160.0 440.0 Td (Cloud Hosting) Tj      (Paints string at x,y) |
| 450.0 440.0 Td ($1,450.00) Tj          (Paints string at x,y) |
+-------------------------------------------------------------+

Because the PDF file itself has no concept of rows, columns, or cell boundaries, any converter must reverse-engineer and hallucinate the table structure entirely from geometric coordinates. When that reverse-engineering fails, your spreadsheet breaks.

2. The 3 Silent Killers in Converted Financial Data

A. The CHAR(160) Non-Breaking Space Trap

This is the single most common cause of =SUM() = 0.

When converters extract horizontal text streams, coordinate gaps between words and numbers are often translated into non-breaking spaces (  or Unicode U+00A0 / ASCII 160) rather than standard ASCII whitespace (CHAR(32)).

To human eyes, 1450.00 and 1450.00 look identical. But to Excel's calculation engine, any cell containing CHAR(160) is strictly classified as a Text String, not a Number. Excel silently ignores text strings inside =SUM(), yielding a grand total of zero without throwing a single error.

B. Accounting Parentheses vs Negative Signs

Financial statements frequently represent negative values using parentheses: (1,450.00) instead of -1,450.00. Naive regex parsers and basic OCR tools either strip the opening parenthesis, misinterpret the brackets as text characters, or drop the negative multiplier altogether, turning debits into credits.

C. Multi-Line Description Drift

If a transaction description wraps over two lines:

  • Line 1: Invoice #9824 - Annual Enterprise
  • Line 2: Software Subscription Renewal

Naive converters interpret each line as a distinct table row. As a result, the numeric amount ($4,800.00) is assigned to Line 1, while Line 2 creates an empty ghost row beneath it, shifting subsequent transactions out of sync with their timestamps.

3. How to Clean Broken Tables in Excel (The Quick Fix)

If you are currently stuck with an Excel sheet where formulas return zero, run these three quick remediation steps:

  1. Purge Non-Breaking Spaces: In a helper column, clean the numeric values using: 
   =VALUE(SUBSTITUTE(CLEAN(A1), CHAR(160), ""))
  1. Convert Text-Formatted Numbers via Text-to-Columns: Select your amount column > Go to the Data tab > Click Text to Columns > Click Finish. This forces Excel to re-evaluate the cell formatting from raw text to floating-point numbers.
  2. Verify with =ISNUMBER(): Before building pivot tables or financial reports, enter =ISNUMBER(E2). If it returns FALSE, the cell still contains hidden typographic artifacts.

4. How Modern Reconstruction Engines Solve Table Extraction

To extract complex tables, bank statements, and invoices without manual data cleaning, modern layout-aware engines use a multi-pass geometric pipeline:

  1. Vertical Projection Profiling: Instead of looking for borders, the engine casts vertical rays down the page to locate whitespace gutters—the natural empty channels between columns that exist even in borderless financial statements.
  2. Horizontal Baseline Clustering: Text tokens are grouped into discrete row buckets based on typographical font baselines, allowing multi-line descriptions within the same vertical envelope to be unified into a single cell.
  3. OpenXML Native AST Generation: When exporting to Word or Excel, the engine outputs genuine , , and structural trees rather than floating text frames.

Summary

Tables in PDFs are an optical illusion. Understanding the difference between coordinate-based PDF paints and semantic document trees is essential for anyone building or managing document automation pipelines.

title: AI Agents Are Trading Real Money Now — Here Is the Verified Record, Not the Hype
summary:
Forget the screenshots. On-chain and venue data from November 2026 shows what AI agents, vaults, and apps actually did with real money — and 17 of 18 advertised claims still can't be checked.

AI agents trading real money is no longer a demo. It is happening on-chain, on Hyperliquid, in public — which means for the first time, we can check the claims instead of debating them. And the verified record, published 2 November 2026 from public chain and venue data, is much more interesting than either the hype or the dismissal.

Here is what it actually shows.

Prediction-market agents: small profit, before costs

Across 312 active AI agents registered on-chain, trading ROI over 90 days was +9.2% — before what they pay for AI predictions. Among agents with enough activity to judge (159 with at least 10 trades), median ROI was +1.6%. The most efficient agents — the 15 making at least $100 per trade — averaged +11.6%, while the least efficient, just 2 agents, averaged −11.5%. Prediction accuracy averaged 60.4%, 10.4 points above chance. On Polymarket, the top AI agents made $1,500–$1,700 in profit over 90 days — enough to show the approach works, not enough to retire on. The best agents were not necessarily the smartest models; they were the ones that traded least often, and wasted least on prediction costs.

AI-labelled vaults: a mixed bag, honestly measured

Of 6 Hyperliquid vaults whose leaders say they are AI-run, 3 beat Bitcoin over the same dates, 2 lost money, and 1 fell more than 30% from a peak. The best stories and the worst drawdowns live in the same table. That is what real trading looks like: not a uniform win, but a spread of outcomes with a real downside. The vaults that survived were not the ones that promised most, but the ones that lost least when they were wrong.

AI trading apps: users mostly lost a little

Across 8 AI trading apps on Hyperliquid, 1,365 users traded $21.0M in 30 days (3 Oct – 1 Nov 2026). In 4 of the 8 apps, users lost money overall, and in most apps fewer than half the users were in profit. The apps are easy to use, the marketing is loud, and the median user still ends the month slightly down. That is the gap between a good demo and a good trade.

AI models with real money: mostly lost

In Nof1's Alpha Arena, where leading models traded real crypto perps, 2 of 6 finished Season 1 with a profit; in Season 1.5, only 5 of 32 accounts did. The best single result was Qwen3 Max at +20.3%; the worst was GPT-5 at −63.4%. And 11.3% of all starting money went to trading fees — 3.7 times the combined profit of the accounts that finished up. Fees are the quiet winner of every AI trading contest.

And the advertised claims?

Of 18 public performance claims checked, 17 had no record anyone else could verify, and 6 were backtests or hypotheticals by the product's own description. A claim without evidence may be true, but it is not a fact. And in trading, the difference between a fact and a story is the difference between a strategy and a sales pitch.

The verdict

The verdict is neither “AI trading works” nor “AI trading is a scam.” It is: some agents make small money, most models lose, fees take a real cut, and nearly every advertised claim is still unverifiable. If the record does not exist, the claim does not either.

That is the same discipline BuildIT Index applies to backtests: recompute from raw data, beat the baselines, survive the folds. The tools change; the standard does not.

If the record does not exist, the claim does not either.

This article is educational, not financial advice. Past results do not predict future returns.

title: Crypto AI Vaults: 3 of 6 Beat Bitcoin, 1 Fell 30% — What That Actually Proves
summary:
The most checkable corner of AI trading is Hyperliquid vaults — public numbers, no screenshots. The results split the hype cleanly in two.

Crypto is where AI trading claims can actually be checked, because Hyperliquid vaults publish their numbers on-chain. No screenshots, no self-reported PnL — just public data. So what does the checkable corner of AI trading actually show?

As of the 2 November 2026 verified check: of 6 Hyperliquid vaults whose leaders say they are AI-run, 3 beat Bitcoin over the same dates, 2 lost money, and 1 fell more than 30% from a peak. Among the vaults passing strict safety and drawdown gates, results ranged from +26.5% (with a −24.2% max drawdown) to −0.1% (with a −10.8% drawdown) — and the top-ranked vault overall, not AI-labelled, returned +24.1% with an −11.9% drawdown while trailing Bitcoin by 4.2 points over the same period.

First, “AI-run” predicts nothing

The label is the operator’s claim, not a performance category. AI-labelled vaults appear across the entire distribution — top, middle, and bottom. If a label predicted returns, the spread would be narrow. It is not. The label tells you what the operator says about their process. It tells you nothing about whether that process works.

Second, beating Bitcoin is the right benchmark — and most don’t

Holding Bitcoin costs nothing, needs no skill, and takes no drawdown decisions. Any vault that trails it over the same dates charged you complexity, fees (typically a 10% profit share for the leader), and drawdown risk for less than doing nothing. Several vaults in the data did exactly that.

Third, drawdown is the story the return hides

A vault up 26.5% that fell 24.2% from a peak is a different proposition from a vault up 8% that fell 3%. The first can wipe out a depositor who arrived at the wrong time; the second is boring in the best way. Rankings by return alone are how people buy the top of a drawdown.

How to evaluate any vault in two minutes

(1) Return vs Bitcoin over the same dates. (2) Max drawdown from peak. (3) Leader’s profit share and stake. (4) How long it has been live (a month of numbers is an anecdote, not a record). (5) Whether deposits are open and what happens in a drawdown — who bears it, you or the leader?

The checkable corner of AI trading does not vindicate the hype or confirm the dismissal. It shows variance: some AI-labelled vaults beat the benchmark, some lose, one fell hard. That variance is the honest answer to “do AI vaults work?” — sometimes, for some operators, with drawdowns that demand respect. Anyone selling you a simpler answer is selling you something else.

title: From Backtest to Funded Account: The Validation Checklist Prop Traders Need Before Paying
summary:
Challenge fees are $200–$1,000+ per attempt, and ~90% of attempts fail. This checklist — run before you pay, not after — is the cheapest money in prop trading.

A prop challenge fee is $200–$1,000+ per attempt, depending on account size. About 90% of attempts fail. That means the average trader pays several fees before ever seeing a funded account — or never does. The cheapest money in prop trading is the validation you run before you pay, not after.

Here is the checklist, in order. Skip a step and you are paying to discover what that step would have told you.

1. Recompute from raw predictions

If your strategy's numbers come from a claimed-accuracy column, a vendor's screenshot, or a backtest you cannot reproduce from raw data, stop. Recompute accuracy from the raw predictions yourself. If the recomputed number is much lower than the claimed one, you just saved a challenge fee.

2. Beat the dumb baselines

Always-bullish and no-change, on the same data. If your model cannot beat both, it adds nothing — it is riding the base rate of up-moves. On a bare CSV with no price history, those two baselines are the honest ones.

3. Check walk-forward folds, not the average

A single overall accuracy hides decay. Demand fold-by-fold results, earliest to latest. A model decaying from 80% to 56% across folds is a dying edge with a flattering average — and it will die faster under challenge pressure.

4. Count the trials and correct for them

How many configurations did you try before this one? If the answer is “hundreds” and no multiple-testing correction was applied, the headline number is partly luck. Apply a Bonferroni-style correction, or at least discount the result honestly.

5. Model costs and slippage

Backtest with realistic spread, slippage, commissions, and taxes. A strategy whose edge survives only at zero friction does not survive.

6. Backtest against the firm's exact rules

Daily drawdown from intraday peaks (5% at FTMO), total drawdown (10%), profit target (10% phase 1, 5% phase 2), minimum trading days. Run the strategy through those constraints historically. If it breaches the daily cap in backtest, it will breach it live — with a fee attached.

7. Size for the worst streak, not the average

Set risk per trade at 0.5–1%, so a normal four-loss streak stays inside the daily cap. Then set a personal daily stop below the firm's cap (stop at 3% down, not 5%).

8. Forward-test on paper first

Two to four weeks of live paper trading under the same rules. Backtesting tells you if a strategy could have worked; forward testing tells you if it actually functions — with real data flow, real fills, and real psychology.

9. Only then, pay

One challenge, sized to the account you can afford to lose the fee on, with the validated strategy and the validated risk parameters.

Most traders do this list backwards: pay first, discover the failures with money. The traders who pass are usually the ones who did the boring work first. Validation is not the opposite of ambition. It is the cheapest form of it.

title: The Daily Drawdown Trap: Why One Bad Morning Ends Your Prop Challenge
summary:
You can be net profitable for two weeks and still fail a prop challenge. Not because your strategy broke. Because one bad morning breached the daily cap — and the challenge does not care about your two good weeks.

The rule most traders misunderstand

FTMO's daily drawdown limit is 5%, calculated from the highest equity point of the day. That “highest equity point” clause is the trap: intraday peaks count against you. If your account peaks 3% up in the morning and then falls 5% from that peak, you have breached the daily limit even though you are only 2% down on the day. Many traders learn this clause only when it eliminates them.

The math that makes it inevitable at normal risk sizes

Risk 2.5% per trade and two consecutive losses end your challenge. Risk 2% and three losers in a row does it. With typical win rates of 45–55%, losing streaks of two, three, and four are not rare events — they are routine occurrences across any meaningful sample of trades. Data from prop-firm analyses puts daily-drawdown breaches behind roughly 70–79% of all evaluation failures. The challenge is not filtering for bad traders. It is filtering for traders whose position sizing cannot survive their own normal losing streaks.

What passers actually do

They risk 0.5–1% per trade — even when the rules allow two or three times that. At 1% risk, a four-loss streak costs 4% and stays inside the daily cap. At 0.5%, it costs 2%. The difference between passing and failing is rarely strategy quality. It is whether a normal bad morning is survivable.

How to survive it (before you pay)

Backtest against the exact rules — daily cap from intraday peaks, total cap, profit target, minimum days — not just for profit.

Size positions so that your worst normal losing streak (not your average streak, your worst) stays inside the daily cap.

Set a personal daily stop below the firm's cap — stop trading at 3% down, not 5%. The buffer is the difference between a bad day and a failed challenge.

Validate the strategy first: recompute from raw predictions, beat the baselines, check walk-forward folds. A strategy that cannot survive its own rules on paper will not survive them with a fee attached.

The daily drawdown trap is not unfair. It is the product: firms sell evaluations, and the evaluation is designed to filter. Knowing the filter exists — and sizing for it — is the entire game. Most traders pay to discover it. You just read it for free.

title: ChatGPT Can’t Backtest: Why “AI” Trading Bots With 10-Year Backtests Are Fiction
summary:
A bot that needs live ChatGPT calls cannot have a 2019 backtest — ChatGPT didn't exist. That single fact exposes most “AI EAs” on the market.

Here is a fact that eliminates most “AI trading bots” on the market in one sentence: a bot whose decisions require live calls to a language model cannot be backtested — because the model did not exist for most of the backtest window.

ChatGPT launched in 2022. A product showing you a flawless 2019 backtest for its “ChatGPT-powered” bot is showing you fiction — or, more charitably, a conventional strategy with AI branding. Real AI decisions require live API connectivity, cost money per call, and take seconds per decision (roughly 3–7 seconds end to end in published breakdowns). You cannot retroactively generate historical decisions from a model that did not exist, and you cannot backtest a system whose response times and model versions change underneath you. GPT-5 thinks differently from GPT-4. A backtest run on one is not evidence about the other.

The five red flags that expose fake AI EAs

Perfect long backtests. Five to ten years of flawless “AI-optimised” results. If the AI did not exist for those years, the backtest is not AI. Period.

No live record. No public wallet, no vault, no exchange-verified account. Only screenshots — which can be cropped from a cherry-picked window.

Hidden recovery systems. “Our AI intelligently scales positions for optimal recovery” is usually a martingale system doubling down on losses, described in softer words.

Annualised short windows. A good fortnight dressed as a triple-digit APR. Always ask: over what window, in what market, net of what fees?

No losing months shown. Every real trading record has losing months. A record without them is a curated exhibit, not a record.

How to validate a real AI trading system, then?

Forward testing. Since backtesting is impossible for genuine LLM-driven bots, the only honest validation is: demo for at least 30 days, then small live capital, with every trade logged and every cost counted. If a vendor refuses forward testing and offers only a backtest, that refusal is the answer.

The broader lesson applies to every trading claim, AI or not: recompute from raw data, beat the baselines, demand the trial count, check the folds. A claim that cannot survive those checks is marketing, whatever technology word is printed on it.

title: Bind an abstract edit to the current source before comparing wording
summary:
A candidate may be a reasonable edit of yesterday's paragraph and still be unsuitable for the paragraph the author has selected today. In an academic editing workflow, preserve that distinction before asking whether the new wording is better.

We are the RigorMed team. The following complete, standard-library Python example was run locally. All text is fictional teaching material. This is a small source-binding demonstration, not a public product API, a manuscript-editing model or a clinical research run.

The input and the decision

The current source is one identified segment: “We evaluated 72 records from a retrospective study.” The candidate carries both its proposed wording and the exact source text it was prepared against. The positive case uses the current sentence. The stale case carries a different source sentence with 68 records.

The function below answers only one question: does this candidate refer to the current segment and carry the exact current source? It does not decide whether the proposed scientific wording is correct.

import json


def bind_candidate(current, candidate):
    key = candidate['segment_id']
    return key in current and current[key] == candidate['source_text']


current = {'seg_0001': 'We evaluated 72 records from a retrospective study.'}
candidate = {
    'segment_id': 'seg_0001',
    'source_text': current['seg_0001'],
    'edited_text': 'A retrospective study evaluated 72 records.',
}
stale = dict(candidate, source_text='We evaluated 68 records from a retrospective study.')
print(json.dumps({
    'current_source_matches': bind_candidate(current, candidate),
    'stale_source_matches': bind_candidate(current, stale),
    'semantic_review_performed': False,
}, indent=2))

The actual output was:

{
  "current_source_matches": true,
  "stale_source_matches": false,
  "semantic_review_performed": false
}

Use the result to route review

The false stale-source result is a reason to stop applying that candidate and regenerate or review it against the current paragraph. Do not silently replace its stored source with the new sentence and keep the old edit: that would conceal the mismatch rather than resolve it.

The true result only establishes the source association. The edited sentence must still be compared with its source. For example, record counts, sample counts and repeated measurements have different meanings; matching a segment identifier does not establish any of those facts.

An integration can present four existing pieces together: the current source, the proposed edit, the stated change reason and unresolved author checks. Keep the source untouched and let the author accept or reject the candidate after reviewing the actual change. An identifier or a text match is not a quality score.

What the larger local precheck demonstrated

In a separate self-written fictional biomedical paragraph, we prepared one candidate that retained 126 adults and one deliberately incorrect candidate that changed 126 to 162. Our existing local academic-text precheck returned REVIEW_REQUIRED for the first, with no blockers and one semantic-review item. The changed-number counterexample returned BLOCKED with two blockers and no edited-text preview.

Those results belong to that separate precheck, not to the small function above. They show how a source-bound handoff and deterministic checks can provide useful review material while still retaining unresolved semantic work. Neither a matching source nor a rule result authorizes submission or establishes scientific validity.

For a real handoff, use text the author is authorized to process, retain the selected segment and editing goal, and ask for changes and unresolved checks alongside the draft. Do not infer missing study facts from a request to improve language.

For an existing academic-text task, the RigorMed research entry is https://rigormed.com/en?utm_source=dev&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=d54_noon_edit_focus . Model use follows displayed credit terms. This article reports the local examples above; it does not claim a new production run, an external Skill integration or measured time savings.

title: Open source AI shorts generators: the repos worth running in 2026
summary:
Most open source AI shorts generators fall into two families: faceless stock-footage pipelines and long-video clippers. Here are five on GitHub with the facts I checked today, what each one does and doesn't do, and where they fall down for code content.

Full disclosure first: I build ReelMint, a closed-source video studio for developers making vertical Shorts, so I have a stake here. This post is for someone who typed "open source ai shorts generator" into a search box and wants to know which repos are real, what they need to run, and whether any of them fit technical content. Stars, licences and last-commit dates below come from the GitHub API on 3 November 2026. Feature details come from each repo's README on the same day. I did not install or benchmark any of them, so I describe what they claim to do, not how well they do it.

What an open source AI shorts generator does (and doesn't)

The category splits into two families, and mixing them up is the most common mistake in search results.

  • Topic to video (faceless pipelines). You give a topic. An LLM writes a script, a TTS engine reads it, stock footage is matched to the sentences, captions are burned in, and an MP4 comes out.
  • Long video to clips. You give a podcast or a YouTube URL. Whisper transcribes it, an LLM picks highlight moments, and the tool crops them to 9:16.

What both families leave to you: editing a finished result, keeping a consistent brand look across videos, and judging whether the content is any good. Most also leave the publishing step half-built, and that last point matters more than it looks (see the YouTube policy section below).

The repos worth running (verified)

All figures below were read from https://api.github.com/repos// on 3 November 2026. Star counts move daily, so treat them as a snapshot.

MoneyPrinterTurbo (harry0703/MoneyPrinterTurbo): MIT, Python, about 137,900 stars, last push 2 Nov 2026. It takes a topic or keyword and generates the script, matches stock footage, adds voiceover, subtitles and background music, and renders an HD video. The README lists a web UI and an API, Docker support (docker compose -f docker-compose.release.yml up, UI on port 8501), and LLM options including OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini and DeepSeek. Edge TTS needs no key; other voice providers need their own. The README says the minimum is 4 CPU cores and 4 GB RAM with no GPU. It lists publishing to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts as a feature but gives no setup details, so check that part yourself before relying on it.

OpenShorts (mutonby/openshorts): MIT, Python, about 7,400 stars, last push 2 Nov 2026. This is the long-video family: it detects moments, reframes with face tracking, adds subtitles and can dub. It also has an AI actor tool and a title and thumbnail tool. Self-hosting is docker compose up --build, then you enter keys in Settings. The README names Gemini as required for the AI features, fal.ai for the AI actor shorts, ElevenLabs for voice and dubbing, and Upload-Post for social posting (TikTok, Reels, YouTube Shorts). It ships an MCP server, at localhost:8000/mcp when self-hosted. There is also a hosted version; the README lists a free plan of 20 minutes a month with a watermark and paid plans from $12 a month.

ShortGPT (RayVentura/ShortGPT): MIT, Python, about 8,100 stars, last push 10 Feb 2025. The repo describes itself as an experimental framework for YouTube Shorts and TikTok channel automation, covering script, voiceover, footage, captions and rendering. I am not calling it abandoned. I am reporting that the last push was in February 2025, and that the README says documentation is still coming. The README does not list required keys, though it names OpenAI, ElevenLabs and Pexels as technologies used.

AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator (SamurAIGPT/AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator): MIT, Python, about 5,700 stars, last push 3 Nov 2026. It is a long-video clipper pitched as an open source alternative to Opus Clip. Give it a YouTube URL and it uses Whisper, an LLM for highlights, and automatic cropping to produce ranked 9:16 clips. API mode needs a MUAPI_API_KEY; local mode needs an OpenAI or Gemini key plus ffmpeg. The README does not mention uploading to YouTube. It also promotes a hosted per-clip API from the same ecosystem.

MoneyPrinterV2 (FujiwaraChoki/MoneyPrinterV2): AGPL-3.0, Python, about 32,300 stars, last push 15 Sep 2026. It bundles several automations, including a scheduled YouTube Shorts automator, a Twitter bot and affiliate tooling, configured through config.json and requiring Python 3.12. The AGPL licence matters if you plan to run a modified version as a service. I could not confirm the upload credentials it needs from the README.

Comparison list

  • MoneyPrinterTurbo: topic to video, MIT, key for an LLM (Edge TTS free), stock footage, active as of 2 Nov 2026.
  • OpenShorts: long video to clips plus extras, MIT, Gemini required, optional fal.ai, ElevenLabs and Upload-Post keys, has an MCP server, active as of 2 Nov 2026.
  • ShortGPT: topic to video framework, MIT, last push Feb 2025, documentation incomplete.
  • AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator: long video to clips, MIT, one API key (MuAPI, or OpenAI/Gemini in local mode), no upload described.
  • MoneyPrinterV2: multi-automation toolkit, AGPL-3.0, config-file driven, last push 15 Sep 2026.

I also looked for n8n and Make templates that wrap these steps. I did not verify any specific template well enough to list it, so I left them out rather than guess.

Automating YouTube Shorts: what YouTube's policy actually says

Developers asking about "youtube shorts automation" usually worry about getting a channel flagged. The relevant text is YouTube's channel monetization policies page, support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392, which I read on 3 November 2026. A July 2025 update on that page renamed the policy from "repetitious content" to "inauthentic content".

What I took from it, in my own words. Automation and AI are not banned. The page says that if you use automated tools or templates, the final product still has to show your creative vision and give viewers educational or entertainment value. The things it names as a problem are content that looks made from a template, and AI content made with generic or unoriginal templates that gives the impression of mass production. Channels whose videos are interchangeable are described as not eligible to monetize. Note the scope: this is about eligibility for the YouTube Partner Program. Content that breaks the Community Guidelines is a separate matter and can be removed. I found no numeric threshold, such as a maximum number of uploads per day, and I won't invent one.

The practical reading for a pipeline: a script written by an LLM from a bare keyword, stock clips, a default voice and the same layout on every video is the pattern the page describes. A video built from your own repo, your own terminal output and your own explanation is not interchangeable with the next channel's. That is a judgement about the content, which no repo can make for you.

Where open-source pipelines fall down for technical content

The topic-to-video family matches stock footage to sentences. Ask it for a video about a Postgres index and you get b-roll of servers and someone typing, not the query plan. There is no step where a real code snippet, a terminal session or a chart is rendered as the visual. The long-video family has the opposite problem: it needs a long recording to exist already, and it crops talking heads, not syntax-highlighted code that must stay legible at 9:16.

Three more gaps show up for developers specifically. First, editing: when scene four has the wrong variable name, you re-run the pipeline or open the MP4 in a separate editor. Second, consistency: nothing carries a code theme, font or colour palette from one video to the next. Third, accuracy: an LLM writing narration over stock footage has nothing checking that the code on screen is the code being described, because no code is on screen. Our own take on the editing problem is in editable AI Shorts generators, and the content side is in YouTube Shorts for developers.

Where ReelMint fits (and that it isn't open source)

ReelMint is not open source. It is a hosted product; you cannot read or self-host the code. What it is: a Remotion-based render pipeline where every generated scene is editable in a visual editor, with code cards, terminal cards and chart animations as scene types. It is driven by an MCP server that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can connect to, with 130+ MCP tools. It is BYOK, meaning you bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs and similar keys, and there is a free tier. It publishes to YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review, so I am not counting it.

On time, the only number I will stand behind: on the MCP path, a 60 to 90 second reel took me 45 to 60 minutes elapsed, of which 10 to 20 minutes were hands-on. That is one person, the person who built it, so a newcomer will be slower.

When ReelMint is not the right pick

  • You need to read or modify the source, or run everything offline on your own hardware. Use MoneyPrinterTurbo or OpenShorts.
  • You have a long recording and want clips from it. Use OpenShorts or AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator. That is not what we do.
  • You want zero-cost faceless channel output from a keyword and do not care about technical accuracy. A stock-footage pipeline is closer to that job.
  • You need a proof or equation animation. That is Manim territory, not ours.

Is there a free open source AI shorts generator?

Yes. MoneyPrinterTurbo, OpenShorts, ShortGPT and AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator are all MIT licensed per the GitHub API on 3 November 2026, and MoneyPrinterV2 is AGPL-3.0. Free to use does not mean free to run: most need at least one LLM key, and some need voice, video or posting keys, billed by those providers.

Can I automate YouTube Shorts with an API?

Partly. OpenShorts documents a REST API and an MCP server, and MoneyPrinterTurbo documents API docs at port 8080 in its Docker setup. Both can generate clips programmatically. Uploading is a separate step handled by YouTube's own APIs or a service like Upload-Post, which OpenShorts uses. I did not test any of these end to end, so verify the upload path before building on it.

Will YouTube penalise auto-generated Shorts?

YouTube's policy page does not ban automation or AI. It says the final video still has to show your creative vision and have educational or entertainment value, and it describes template-made, mass-produced, interchangeable content as ineligible for monetization. It reads as a monetization policy, not a ban on uploading. I found no stated upload-volume threshold.

If your content is technical, the easier route to non-interchangeable videos is to put real code and real output on screen. You can try that with the code explainer Shorts maker on the free tier.

Originally published on reelmint.io.

Developers asking about "youtube shorts automation" usually worry about getting a channel flagged. The relevant text is YouTube's channel monetization policies page, support.google.com/youtube/answer/1311392, which I read on 3 November 2026. A July 2025 update on that page renamed the policy from "repetitious content" to "inauthentic content".

What I took from it, in my own words. Automation and AI are not banned. The page says that if you use automated tools or templates, the final product still has to show your creative vision and give viewers educational or entertainment value. The things it names as a problem are content that looks made from a template, and AI content made with generic or unoriginal templates that gives the impression of mass production. Channels whose videos are interchangeable are described as not eligible to monetize. Note the scope: this is about eligibility for the YouTube Partner Program. Content that breaks the Community Guidelines is a separate matter and can be removed. I found no numeric threshold, such as a maximum number of uploads per day, and I won't invent one.

The practical reading for a pipeline: a script written by an LLM from a bare keyword, stock clips, a default voice and the same layout on every video is the pattern the page describes. A video built from your own repo, your own terminal output and your own explanation is not interchangeable with the next channel's. That is a judgement about the content, which no repo can make for you.

Where open-source pipelines fall down for technical content

The topic-to-video family matches stock footage to sentences. Ask it for a video about a Postgres index and you get b-roll of servers and someone typing, not the query plan. There is no step where a real code snippet, a terminal session or a chart is rendered as the visual. The long-video family has the opposite problem: it needs a long recording to exist already, and it crops talking heads, not syntax-highlighted code that must stay legible at 9:16.

Three more gaps show up for developers specifically. First, editing: when scene four has the wrong variable name, you re-run the pipeline or open the MP4 in a separate editor. Second, consistency: nothing carries a code theme, font or colour palette from one video to the next. Third, accuracy: an LLM writing narration over stock footage has nothing checking that the code on screen is the code being described, because no code is on screen. Our own take on the editing problem is in editable AI Shorts generators, and the content side is in YouTube Shorts for developers.

Where ReelMint fits (and that it isn't open source)

ReelMint is not open source. It is a hosted product; you cannot read or self-host the code. What it is: a Remotion-based render pipeline where every generated scene is editable in a visual editor, with code cards, terminal cards and chart animations as scene types. It is driven by an MCP server that Claude Desktop, Claude Code and Cursor can connect to, with 130+ MCP tools. It is BYOK, meaning you bring your own OpenAI, Anthropic, ElevenLabs and similar keys, and there is a free tier. It publishes to YouTube Shorts. Instagram Reels publishing is pending Meta App Review, so I am not counting it.

On time, the only number I will stand behind: on the MCP path, a 60 to 90 second reel took me 45 to 60 minutes elapsed, of which 10 to 20 minutes were hands-on. That is one person, the person who built it, so a newcomer will be slower.

When ReelMint is not the right pick

  • You need to read or modify the source, or run everything offline on your own hardware. Use MoneyPrinterTurbo or OpenShorts.
  • You have a long recording and want clips from it. Use OpenShorts or AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator. That is not what we do.
  • You want zero-cost faceless channel output from a keyword and do not care about technical accuracy. A stock-footage pipeline is closer to that job.
  • You need a proof or equation animation. That is Manim territory, not ours.

Is there a free open source AI shorts generator?

Yes. MoneyPrinterTurbo, OpenShorts, ShortGPT and AI-Youtube-Shorts-Generator are all MIT licensed per the GitHub API on 3 November 2026, and MoneyPrinterV2 is AGPL-3.0. Free to use does not mean free to run: most need at least one LLM key, and some need voice, video or posting keys, billed by those providers.

Can I automate YouTube Shorts with an API?

Partly. OpenShorts documents a REST API and an MCP server, and MoneyPrinterTurbo documents API docs at port 8080 in its Docker setup. Both can generate clips programmatically. Uploading is a separate step handled by YouTube's own APIs or a service like Upload-Post, which OpenShorts uses. I did not test any of these end to end, so verify the upload path before building on it.

Will YouTube penalise auto-generated Shorts?

YouTube's policy page does not ban automation or AI. It says the final video still has to show your creative vision and have educational or entertainment value, and it describes template-made, mass-produced, interchangeable content as ineligible for monetization. It reads as a monetization policy, not a ban on uploading. I found no stated upload-volume threshold.

If your content is technical, the easier route to non-interchangeable videos is to put real code and real output on screen. You can try that with the code explainer Shorts maker on the free tier.
